artworks.title: Jupiter and Lycaon (Júpiter y Licaón)
artworks.description: This dramatic Flemish Baroque canvas in the Museo del Prado depicts the impiety of Lycaon, the son and successor of Pelasgus, first king of Arcadia. Cossiers stages the moment from Book I of Ovid's Metamorphoses when Lycaon, having served human flesh to test the divinity of his guest, is exposed by Jupiter: the god rises in wrath as his eagle hurls thunderbolts, while Lycaon springs from the banquet table, his head already contorting into that of a wolf. Through the Arcadian dynasty that Pelasgus founded — Pelasgus invented huts, sheepskin garments, and the acorn diet before his son Lycaon advanced his ambitions — the painting visualizes the cursed lineage descended from Arcadia's first man.

artworks.title: Lycaon Transformed into a Wolf
artworks.description: An engraving from Hendrik Goltzius's illustrated edition of Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book I, plate 9), now in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. It shows Jupiter transforming Lycaon — son of Pelasgus, the autochthonous first king of Arcadia — into a wolf as punishment for his blasphemous feast. Goltzius captures the metamorphosis in mid-motion, the king's body bristling with fur as he flees on all fours while Jupiter presides over the scene. The print belongs to the broader iconography of Pelasgus's Arcadian house, whose mythic founder is rarely portrayed alone and is most often evoked through the fate of his notorious son.

artworks.title: Jupiter and Lycaon
artworks.description: A French Renaissance relief by Hugues Sambin stages Zeus's wrath against Lycaon, son of Pelasgus of Arcadia: the impious king who served human flesh is caught at the moment of divine judgment that will turn him into a wolf. As with the Cossiers canvas and Goltzius plate, the scene visualizes the cursed heir of Arcadia's first king — Pelasgus himself remaining almost without freestanding portraiture, his house remembered through Lycaon's metamorphosis.
